On a conjecture of distance spectral extremal problems

Hongzhang Chen ††thanks: School of Mathematics and Statistics, Gansu Center for Applied Mathematics, Lanzhou University, Lanzhou, Gansu, 730000, China. Email: mnhzchern@gmail.com.    Jianxi Li ††thanks: School of Mathematics and Statistics, Minnan Normal University, Zhangzhou, Fujian, 363000, China. Email: ptjxli@hotmail.com. Partially supported by the NSF of Fujian Province (No. 2021J02048).    Yongtao Li ††thanks: Corresponding author. Yau Mathematical Sciences Center, Tsinghua University, Beijing, 100084, China. Email: ytli0921@hnu.edu.cn.
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Brualdi and Hoffman proposed a well-known problem of determining the graph with maximum adjacency spectral radius among all graphs with given size mm. Early work by Friedland and Stanley addressed some specific cases. This problem was later completely solved by Rowlinson and recently revisited by Cheng and Weng. Pioneering work on the distance matrix was carried out by Graham and Pollak, as well as by Graham and Lovász. The distance spectral radius ρ⁡(G)\rho(G) of a connected graph GG is the largest eigenvalue of its distance matrix.

In this paper, we completely solve the problem of characterizing the connected graph with minimum distance spectral radius among all graphs with size mm. Let 𝒢⁡(m)\mathcal{G}(m) be the class of connected graphs with mm edges. For every m⩾3m\geqslant 3, let nn be the unique integer satisfying (n−12)<m⩽(n2)\binom{n-1}{2}<m\leqslant\binom{n}{2}, and we write m=(n−12)+sm=\binom{n-1}{2}+s with 1⩽s⩽n−11\leqslant s\leqslant n-1. Recently, Lin and Zhou [Adv. in Appl. Math. 173 (2026)] investigated the graph in 𝒢⁡(m)\mathcal{G}(m) that minimizes ρ⁡(G)\rho(G) in the range s⩾max⁡{n−62,1}s\geqslant\max\{\frac{n-6}{2},1\}. However, the problem is much more difficult in the remaining range 1⩽s⩽n−721\leqslant s\leqslant\frac{n-7}{2}, and they conjectured that the unique minimizer is Pn,s+1¯\overline{P_{n,s+1}}, the complement of a balanced disjoint union of paths. Using novel matrix analysis, we solve this conjecture in the affirmative. Moreover, we provide a new unified proof for the entire range 1⩽s⩽n−11\leqslant s\leqslant n-1.

The key ingredients in our proof argument include an innovative comparison principle for the distance spectral radius, an increment analysis of Φ\Phi-functions on paths and cycles, an argument for balancing path lengths, and a walk enumeration technique via the Neumann series.

Key words: Distance spectral radius, Lin–Zhou’s conjecture.

2020 AMS Subject Classifications: 05C50, 05C35.

1 Introduction

Let GG be a simple connected graph with vertex set V⁡(G)V(G) and edge set E⁡(G)E(G). We denote by nn and e⁡(G)e(G) the order and size of GG, respectively. The complement of GG is denoted as G¯\overline{G}. For any vertex u∈V⁡(G)u\in V(G), let dG​(u)d_{G}(u) and NG​(u)N_{G}(u) (or d⁡(u)d(u) and N⁡(u)N(u) for short) be the degree and the set of neighbors of uu, respectively. Clearly, dG​(u)=|NG​(u)|d_{G}(u)=|N_{G}(u)|. We write 𝟏\mathbf{1} for the all-ones column vector and J=𝟏𝟏𝖳J=\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}} for the all-ones matrix. Let II be the identity matrix. We denote by CℓC_{\ell} the cycle on ℓ\ell vertices, and PkP_{k} the path on kk vertices. The adjacency matrix of an nn-vertex graph GG is defined as A⁡(G)=[ai​j]i,j=1nA(G)=[a_{ij}]_{i,j=1}^{n}, where ai​j=1a_{ij}=1 if i​j∈E⁡(G)ij\in E(G), and ai​j=0a_{ij=0} otherwise. The spectral radius λ⁡(G)\lambda(G) of a graph GG is defined as the largest eigenvalue of its adjacency matrix A⁡(G)A(G).

1.1 The Brualdi–Hoffman type extremal problem

The study of bounding the spectral radius of a graph in terms of the number of edges has a long and rich history. It is well-known that λ⁡(G)<2​m\lambda(G)<\sqrt{2m}. Tracking back to 1985, Brualdi and Hoffman [4] proved that if GG has m⩽(k2)m\leqslant{k\choose 2} edges for some integer k⩾2k\geqslant 2, then λ⁡(G)⩽k−1\lambda(G)\leqslant k-1. This bound was further extended by Friedland [7], and later by Stanley [22] who showed that λ​(G)⩽12​(8​m+1−1)\lambda(G)\leqslant\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{8m+1}-1), with equality if and only if m=(k2)m={k\choose 2} and GG is a complete graph KkK_{k}. Here, we ignore the possible isolated vertices if there are no confusions. We write m=(s2)+tm={s\choose 2}+t for some integers s,ts,t with 0⩽t⩽s−10\leqslant t\leqslant s-1. Let K1∨tKsK_{1}\vee_{t}K_{s} be the graph obtained from KsK_{s} by adding a new vertex joining tt vertices of KsK_{s}. In 1988, Rowlinson [19] proved that if GG has mm edges, then λ(G)⩽λ(K1∨tKs)\lambda(G)\leqslant\lambda(K_{1}\vee_{t}K_{s}), with equality if and only if G=K1∨tKsG=K_{1}\vee_{t}K_{s}. This confirms a conjecture proposed by Brualdi and Hoffman [4]. Roughly speaking, the graph with the largest adjacency spectral radius packs almost all edges into the clique, and then attaches the remaining edges to that clique. We refer to [5] for a matrix realization of these spectral bounds.

Motivated by the Turán theorem, Nikiforov [18] significantly improved the above bounds by proving that if GG is a Kr+1K_{r+1}-free graph, then λ2​(G)⩽(1−1r)​2​m\lambda^{2}(G)\leqslant(1-\frac{1}{r})2m. In particular, this recovers a result of Nosal, saying that every mm-edge triangle-free GG satisfies λ⁡(G)⩽m\lambda(G)\leqslant\sqrt{m}. For related results, we refer the readers to [12, 11, 13]. Recently, Li, Liu and Zhang [14] proved that for any graph FF with chromatic number r+1⩾3r+1\geqslant 3, if GG is an FF-free graph with mm edges, then λ2​(G)⩽(1−1r+o⁡(1))​2​m\lambda^{2}(G)\leqslant\big(1-\frac{1}{r}+o(1)\big)2m. Extending Nikiforov’s theorem, Li, Liu and Zhang [15] proved that the o⁡(1)o(1) error term can be removed for color-critical graphs FF; and λ⁡(G)⩽m+O⁡(1)\lambda(G)\leqslant\sqrt{m}+O(1) for almost-bipartite graphs FF.

1.2 The distance spectral extremal problem

The distance between two vertices u,vu,v, denoted by dG​(u,v)d_{G}(u,v), is the length of a shortest path connecting them. The distance matrix of GG is defined as D⁡(G)=(dG​(u,v))u,v∈V⁡(G)D(G)=(d_{G}(u,v))_{u,v\in V(G)}. The distance spectral radius ρ⁡(G)\rho(G) is defined as the largest eigenvalue of D⁡(G)D(G). Note that D⁡(G)D(G) is nonnegative and irreducible. By the Perron–Frobenius theorem, ρ⁡(G)\rho(G) is a positive simple eigenvalue, and there exists a unique positive unit eigenvector corresponding to ρ⁡(G)\rho(G). The study of eigenvalues of the distance matrix of a connected graph dates back to the classical work [8, 9, 10], where they provided an inequality related the number of negative distance eigenvalues to the addressing problem in data communication system. The properties of distance matrix turn out to be significant in the study of the isometric embedding problems from a connected graph to the squashed hypercube; see [23, 21, 1]. We refer to the comprehensive surveys [2, 16] for recent development.

For connected graphs of fixed order nn, the extremal problems are classical: Ruzieh and Powers [20] and Stevanović and Ilić [24] showed that the complete graph KnK_{n} uniquely minimizes ρ\rho, while the path PnP_{n} uniquely maximizes ρ\rho. In contrast, the adjacency spectral radius exhibits the opposite behavior: the complete graph KnK_{n} is the unique maximizer, and the path PnP_{n} is the unique minimizer. Here, we provide an explanation for this reversed phenomenon. The adjacency spectral radius λ⁡(G)\lambda(G) measures how well a graph expands or how strongly it is connected: a large value indicates a dense graph with many edges and small diameter (e.g., a clique). In contrast, the distance spectral radius ρ⁡(G)\rho(G) measures the overall separation among vertices: a large value means many pairs of vertices are far apart, so the graph is sparse (e.g., a path or a star). Hence, dense graphs tend to have large λ⁡(G)\lambda(G) but small ρ⁡(G)\rho(G), while sparse graphs tend to have small λ⁡(G)\lambda(G) but large ρ⁡(G)\rho(G).

A much harder problem is to find the extremal graphs among all connected graphs with a prescribed number of edges mm, which was initiated by Lin and Zhou [17]. Let 𝒢⁡(m)\mathcal{G}(m) denote the class of such graphs. Throughout this paper, for a given m⩾3m\geqslant 3, we denote

n:=⌈1+8​m+12⌉,s:=m−(n−12)∈{1,2,…,n−1}.n:=\Bigl\lceil\tfrac{1+\sqrt{8m+1}}{2}\Bigr\rceil,\qquad s:=m-\binom{n-1}{2}\in\{1,2,\ldots,n-1\}. (1)

For positive integers N⩾c⩾1N\geqslant c\geqslant 1, we define

PN,c:=(c+c⁡⌊N/c⌋−N)​P⌊N/c⌋∪(N−c⁡⌊N/c⌋)​P⌈N/c⌉,P_{N,c}\,:=\;\bigl(c+c\lfloor N/c\rfloor-N\bigr)\,P_{\lfloor N/c\rfloor}\;\cup\;\bigl(N-c\lfloor N/c\rfloor\bigr)\,P_{\lceil N/c\rceil},

the balanced disjoint union of cc paths on NN vertices (its parts differ in order by at most one). By the definition, it is easy to verify that Pn,s+1¯\overline{P_{n,s+1}} contains (n2)−(n−s−1)=(n−12)+s=m{n\choose 2}-(n-s-1)={n-1\choose 2}+s=m edges. Intuitively, we see that Pn,s+1¯\overline{P_{n,s+1}} is close to almost-complete graph, which is obtained from the largest possible KnK_{n} by deleting the edges of those s+1s+1 balanced vertex-disjoint paths.

Recently, Lin and Zhou [17, Theorem 1.3] proved that if max⁡{n−62,1}⩽s⩽n−1\max\{\frac{n-6}{2},1\}\leqslant s\leqslant n-1, then Pn,s+1¯\overline{P_{n,s+1}} is the unique graph that minimizes the distance spectral radius over all graphs in 𝒢⁡(m)\mathcal{G}(m). In the concluding remarks of [17], they conjectured that the same formula holds for all small ss.

Conjecture 1.1 (Lin–Zhou [17]).

Let GG be a graph with mm edges, and let nn and ss be defined as in (1). If 1⩽s⩽n−721\leqslant s\leqslant\frac{n-7}{2}, then ρ⁡(G)⩾ρ⁡(Pn,s+1¯),\rho(G)\geqslant\rho\bigl(\overline{P_{n,s+1}}\bigr), with equality if and only if G≅Pn,s+1¯G\cong\overline{P_{n,s+1}}.

In this paper, we resolve Conjecture 1.1 by showing the following result.

Theorem 1.2.

Let G∈𝒢⁡(m)G\in\mathcal{G}(m) minimize ρ\rho of graphs in 𝒢⁡(m)\mathcal{G}(m), and let n=⌈12​(1+8​m+1)⌉n=\lceil\frac{1}{2}(1+\sqrt{8m+1})\rceil and s=m−(n−12)s=m-\binom{n-1}{2}. If 1⩽s<n−221\leqslant s<\frac{n-2}{2}, then G≅Pn,s+1¯G\cong\overline{P_{n,s+1}}. In particular, Conjecture 1.1 holds.

Remark. In the case s=0s=0, the above result is invalid. In this setting, we have m=(n−12)m={n-1\choose 2}, the minimizer is uniquely the complete graph Kn−1K_{n-1}, instead of the expected graph Pn,1¯=Pn¯\overline{P_{n,1}}=\overline{P_{n}}.

The range max⁡{n−62,1}⩽s⩽n−1\max\{\frac{n-6}{2},1\}\leqslant s\leqslant n-1 was already investigated by Lin and Zhou [17], which together with the range in Theorem 1.2 yields the following complete solution of the distance spectral extremal problem for graphs with given size mm.

Theorem 1.3.

For every integer m⩾3m\geqslant 3, let n=⌈12​(1+8​m+1)⌉n=\lceil\frac{1}{2}(1+\sqrt{8m+1})\rceil and s=m−(n−12)s=m-\binom{n-1}{2}. Then for all 1⩽s⩽n−11\leqslant s\leqslant n-1, the graph Pn,s+1¯\overline{P_{n,s+1}} uniquely minimizes ρ\rho over all graphs in 𝒢⁡(m)\mathcal{G}(m).

As an application of our framework, we shall provide a new self-contained proof for s⩾n−22s\geqslant\frac{n-2}{2} in Section 3, thereby giving a unified treatment of Theorem 1.3 for the entire range 1⩽s⩽n−11\leqslant s\leqslant n-1.

Before the proof, we first illustrate the difficulty for the small ss. To appreciate why the range of small ss was much difficult and left open, we now recall how the proof argument of [17, Theorem 1.3] worked for large ss. A structural lemma (we state it as in Theorem 2.1 below) shows that any minimizer GG has complement G¯=Cℓ1∪⋯∪Cℓt∪Pk1∪⋯∪Pks+1\overline{G}=C_{\ell_{1}}\cup\cdots\cup C_{\ell_{t}}\cup P_{k_{1}}\cup\cdots\cup P_{k_{s+1}}, where ℓi⩾3\ell_{i}\geqslant 3, kj⩾2k_{j}\geqslant 2 and the number of path components equals s+1s+1. The problem is therefore to show that the extremal graph is t=0t=0 together with the balanced path partition Pn,s+1P_{n,s+1}. Lin and Zhou’s argument proceeds by local edge-switching: given two candidate configurations, one exchanges a single edge and uses a Rayleigh quotient to show ρ\rho strictly decreases. For large ss, this works well because the number of candidate configurations is small and can be enumerated. In fact, when s=⌈12​(n−5)⌉s=\lceil\frac{1}{2}(n-5)\rceil, the only cyclic candidate is C3∪n−32​K2C_{3}\cup\tfrac{n-3}{2}K_{2}, and a single edge-switch to Pn,(n−3)/2P_{n,(n-3)/2} suffices.

However, when ss is small, the number of possible cycle structures grows without bound, and as one can verify numerically, no single step edge-switch is monotone. There exist cyclic configurations GG such that every local rearrangement, which breaks one cycle and reconnects one path, either fails to be admissible or increases ρ\rho. The following example with n=11n=11 and s=1s=1 illustrates this.

ρ⁡(C3∪P4∪P4¯)≈11.65444,ρ⁡(P3∪P8¯)≈11.65452.\rho(\overline{C_{3}\cup P_{4}\cup P_{4}})\approx 11.65444,\qquad\rho(\overline{P_{3}\cup P_{8}})\approx 11.65452.

The natural operation, which breaks the C3C_{3} into P3P_{3} and merges the two P4P_{4}’s into P8P_{8}, increases the value of ρ\rho, even though the minimum ρ⁡(P11,2¯)=ρ⁡(P5∪P6¯)≈11.65442\rho(\overline{P_{11,2}})=\rho(\overline{P_{5}\cup P_{6}})\approx 11.65442 is strictly smaller than both of the above two graphs. In other words, the minimum can not be reached by a monotone sequence of single-step improvements of the edge-switch operation. To overcome the difficulty, a global argument to compare the distance spectral radii of graphs is required.

Our approach.

We get rid of the use of local edge-switching operations as it fails to be monotone for small integer ss. Instead, we develop a new global comparison framework grounded from matrix analysis. Our approach can be partitioned into three stages.

The first stage lies in linking the distance matrix D⁡(G)D(G) to the adjacency matrix A⁡(H0)A(H_{0}) of the complement H0=G¯H_{0}=\overline{G}. We show an identity D⁡(G)=J−I+A⁡(H0)D(G)=J-I+A(H_{0}), and that ρ⁡(G)\rho(G) is the unique root of the equation 𝟏𝖳​((ρ+1)​I−A⁡(H0))−1​𝟏=1\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}((\rho+1)I-A(H_{0}))^{-1}\mathbf{1}=1; see Lemma 2.3. For a graph KK, we denote ΦK​(λ):=𝟏𝖳​(λ​I−A⁡(K))−1​𝟏\Phi_{K}(\lambda):=\bm{1}^{\mathsf{T}}(\lambda I-A(K))^{-1}\bm{1}. Let 𝒞⁡(H0)\mathcal{C}(H_{0}) be the set of components of H0H_{0}. We define the Ψ\Psi-function of GG as ΨG​(λ):=∑K∈𝒞⁡(H0)ΦK​(λ)\Psi_{G}(\lambda):=\sum_{K\in\mathcal{C}(H_{0})}\Phi_{K}(\lambda); see Definition 2.4. Under the above notation, we reduce the problem of comparing distance spectral radii to evaluating these Ψ\Psi-functions; see Theorem 2.5.

The second stage is to compute the explicit formula of ΦK​(λ)\Phi_{K}(\lambda) when KK is chosen as a path and cycle; see Lemma 2.6. Based on these formulas, we then perform a rigorous increment analysis of ΦK​(λ)\Phi_{K}(\lambda) when KK is a path. We provide an upper bound on the increment and establish a strict convexity property, showing that the map k↦ΦPk​(λ)k\mapsto\Phi_{P_{k}}(\lambda) is strictly convex on kk; see Theorem 2.7.

The third stage is an argument for balancing path lengths. The properties from the second stage allow us to formulate balancing principles, demonstrating that the complement H0H_{0} of the extremal graph must consist exclusively of paths of nearly equal lengths; see Lemma 2.8 and Claim 2.1. Moreover, we show that H0H_{0} must be devoid of any cycles; see Lemma 2.9 and Claim 2.2.

Finally, we present a short self-contained proof in the range s⩾n−22s\geqslant\frac{n-2}{2}. By expanding the Ψ\Psi-function via the Neumann series, we see that ΨG​(λ)=∑k=0∞wk​(H0)λk+1\Psi_{G}(\lambda)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{w_{k}(H_{0})}{\lambda^{k+1}}, where wk​(H0)w_{k}(H_{0}) denotes the total number of walks of length kk in H0H_{0}, we integrate the comparison principle in Theorem 2.5 with walk enumeration to provide a new unified proof covering the entire range 1⩽s⩽n−11\leqslant s\leqslant n-1.

We anticipate that the method developed in this paper will offer an efficient approach to solving additional extremal problems related to graphs and their distance spectral radii.

2 Proof of the main result

In order to prove Theorem 1.2, we need to present some preliminary results. In the range 1⩽s<n−221\leqslant s<\frac{n-2}{2}, the expected extremal graphs in 𝒢⁡(m)\mathcal{G}(m) are restricted by the following result.

Theorem 2.1 (Lin–Zhou [17]).

Let G∈𝒢⁡(m)G\in\mathcal{G}(m) be a graph that minimizes ρ\rho of graphs in 𝒢⁡(m)\mathcal{G}(m). Then |V⁡(G)|=n|V(G)|=n. In addition, if 1⩽s<n−221\leqslant s<\frac{n-2}{2}, then each component of G¯\overline{G} is either a cycle or a non-trivial path, and there are exactly s+1s+1 components being paths in G¯\overline{G}.

Throughout the rest of the paper, we denote by

H0=G¯=Cℓ1∪⋯∪Cℓt∪Pk1∪⋯∪Pks+1,H_{0}=\overline{G}=C_{\ell_{1}}\cup\cdots\cup C_{\ell_{t}}\;\cup\;P_{k_{1}}\cup\cdots\cup P_{k_{s+1}},

where t⩾0,ℓi⩾3,kj⩾2t\geqslant 0,\ \ell_{i}\geqslant 3,\ k_{j}\geqslant 2 satisfying Nc:=∑i=1tℓiN_{c}:=\sum_{i=1}^{t}\ell_{i} and Np:=∑j=1s+1kj=n−Nc.N_{p}:=\sum_{j=1}^{s+1}k_{j}=n-N_{c}. Based on this result, our goal is to prove that t=0t=0 (no cycles) and the path lengths k1,k2,…,ks+1k_{1},k_{2},\ldots,k_{s+1} are as equal as possible. We point out that this is not as easy as it looks. To achieve this goal, we need to establish a series of important lemmas and theorems. We will now present them one by one.

The following lemma from Matrix Analysis can be found in [3, page 7].

Lemma 2.2 (Neumann series, e.g., [3]).

Let A∈ℂn×nA\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n} be a square matrix. If ‖A‖<1\|A\|<1 for some matrix norm (or equivalently, the spectral radius λ⁡(A)<1\lambda(A)<1), then I−AI-A is invertible and

(I−A)−1=∑i=0∞Ai=I+A+A2+A3+⋯(I-A)^{-1}=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}A^{i}=I+A+A^{2}+A^{3}+\cdots

where the series converges in any matrix norm.

2.1 New comparison principle via matrix analysis

The next lemma is the cornerstone of our approach. We establish an interesting relation between the distance spectral radius ρ⁡(G)\rho(G) and the adjacency matrix of H0H_{0}. The diameter of a connected graph GG is defined to be the maximum distance between any two vertices in GG.

Lemma 2.3.

Let H0H_{0} be a disjoint union of cycles and paths, with at least two components, and let G=H0¯G=\overline{H_{0}} on n⩾4n\geqslant 4 vertices. Let A⁡(H0)A(H_{0}) be the adjacency matrix of H0H_{0}. Then

  1. (i)

    GG is connected with diameter exactly 22, and D⁡(G)=J−I+A⁡(H0)D(G)=J-I+A(H_{0}).

  2. (ii)

    ρ:=ρ⁡(G)\rho:=\rho(G) is the unique root in (2,∞)(2,\infty) of the equation

    𝟏𝖳​((ρ+1)​I−A⁡(H0))−1​𝟏=1.\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}\bigl((\rho+1)I-A(H_{0})\bigr)^{-1}\mathbf{1}=1. (2)
  3. (iii)

    Every entry of (λ​I−A⁡(H0))−1\bigl(\lambda I-A(H_{0})\bigr)^{-1} is positive and strictly decreasing in λ\lambda on (2,∞)(2,\infty). In particular, the left-hand side of (2) is strictly decreasing in ρ\rho.

Proof of (i).

By definition, it is easy to see that GG is a connected graph with diameter 22. For any two distinct u,v∈V⁡(G)u,v\in V(G), we see that dG​(u,v)=1d_{G}(u,v)=1 if and only if u​v∉E⁡(H0)uv\notin E(H_{0}); and dG​(u,v)=2d_{G}(u,v)=2 if and only if u​v∈E⁡(H0)uv\in E(H_{0}). Thus, it follows that

dG(u,v)=1+𝟏{uv∈E(H0)}=(J−I)u​v+(A(H0))u​v.d_{G}(u,v)=1+\mathbf{1}_{\{uv\in E(H_{0})\}}\;=\;(J-I)_{uv}+(A(H_{0}))_{uv}.

For u=vu=v, both sides are 00. Hence, we obtain D⁡(G)=J−I+A⁡(H0)D(G)=J-I+A(H_{0}), as needed.

Proof of (ii). Since D⁡(G)D(G) is irreducible and nonnegative, the Perron–Frobenius theorem yields a strictly positive eigenvector 𝒙>0\bm{x}>0 associated with ρ\rho. Normalize so that 𝟏𝖳​𝒙=1\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{x}=1. From part (i),

ρ​𝒙=D⁡(G)​𝒙=(J−I+A⁡(H0))​𝒙=𝟏​(𝟏𝖳​𝒙)−𝒙+A⁡(H0)​𝒙=𝟏−𝒙+A⁡(H0)​𝒙.\rho\,\bm{x}=D(G)\bm{x}=\big(J-I+A(H_{0})\big)\bm{x}=\mathbf{1}(\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{x})-\bm{x}+A(H_{0})\bm{x}=\mathbf{1}-\bm{x}+A(H_{0})\bm{x}.

Rearranging the above gives

((ρ+1)​I−A⁡(H0))​𝒙=𝟏.\bigl((\rho+1)I-A(H_{0})\bigr)\bm{x}=\mathbf{1}. (3)

We next show that the matrix (ρ+1)​I−A⁡(H0)(\rho+1)I-A(H_{0}) is invertible. Since every component KK of H0H_{0} is a cycle or a path, the spectral radius λ⁡(H0)⩽2\lambda(H_{0})\leqslant 2. Since each vertex has degH0⁡(u)⩾1\deg_{H_{0}}(u)\geqslant 1, we have degG⁡(u)⩽n−2\deg_{G}(u)\leqslant n-2. On the other hand, since GG has diameter 22, every row sum of D⁡(G)D(G) equals to 2​(n−1)−degG⁡(u)⩾n2(n-1)-\deg_{G}(u)\geqslant n. By the Perron–Frobenius theorem, we have ρ⁡(G)⩾n⩾4\rho(G)\geqslant n\geqslant 4. Therefore ρ+1⩾n+1>2⩾λ⁡(H0)\rho+1\geqslant n+1>2\geqslant\lambda(H_{0}), and (ρ+1)​I−A⁡(H0)(\rho+1)I-A(H_{0}) is invertible. Solving (3) yields

𝒙=((ρ+1)​I−A⁡(H0))−1​𝟏.\bm{x}=\big((\rho+1)I-A(H_{0})\big)^{-1}\mathbf{1}.

multiplying 𝟏𝖳\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}} of both sides and using the assumption 𝟏𝖳​𝒙=1\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{x}=1 gives the desired identity (2).

Proof of (iii). For λ>2⩾λ⁡(H0)\lambda>2\geqslant\lambda(H_{0}), the Neumann series in Lemma 2.2 gives

(λ​I−A⁡(H0))−1=∑i=0∞A​(H0)iλi+1,\big(\lambda I-A(H_{0})\big)^{-1}=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\frac{A(H_{0})^{i}}{\lambda^{i+1}},

where the series converges entrywise. Since A⁡(H0)A(H_{0}) is nonnegative, each entry of the partial sums is a nonnegative, strictly decreasing function of λ\lambda, and the same holds in the limit. In particular, the left-hand side of (2) equals ∑i=0∞λ−(i+1)​𝟏𝖳​A​(H0)i​𝟏\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\lambda^{-(i+1)}\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}A(H_{0})^{i}\mathbf{1}, whose i=0i=0 term nλ\frac{n}{\lambda} is already strictly decreasing, so the whole sum is strictly decreasing in λ\lambda on (2,∞)(2,\infty). This proves (iii), and together with the identity (2) at λ=ρ+1\lambda=\rho+1, also show that (2) has a unique root in (2,∞)(2,\infty). ∎

For each component KK of H0H_{0} and λ>2\lambda>2, we define

ΦK​(λ):=𝟏𝖳​(λ​I−A⁡(K))−1​𝟏.\Phi_{K}(\lambda):=\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}\bigl(\lambda I-A(K)\bigr)^{-1}\mathbf{1}.

Next, we extend the notation to the graph H0H_{0}. Since A⁡(H0)A(H_{0}) is block-diagonal with each block corresponding to a component of H0H_{0}, its inverse matrix (λ​I−A⁡(H0))−1(\lambda I-A(H_{0}))^{-1} is also block-diagonal.

Definition 2.4.

Let H0=G¯H_{0}=\overline{G} be a disjoint union of cycles and paths, with at least two components. Denote 𝒞⁡(H0)\mathcal{C}(H_{0}) the set of components of H0H_{0}. We define the Ψ\Psi-function of GG as follows:

ΨG​(λ):=ΦH0​(λ)=∑K∈𝒞⁡(H0)ΦK​(λ).\Psi_{G}(\lambda):=\Phi_{H_{0}}(\lambda)=\sum_{K\in\mathcal{C}(H_{0})}\Phi_{K}(\lambda).

Thus, Lemma 2.3 (ii) gives ΨG​(ρ⁡(G)+1)=1\Psi_{G}(\rho(G)+1)=1. Lemma 2.3 (iii) implies that ΦH0​(λ)\Phi_{H_{0}}(\lambda) is strictly decreasing in λ∈(2,∞)\lambda\in(2,\infty). By Definition 2.4, we know that ΨG​(λ)\Psi_{G}(\lambda) is also strictly decreasing in λ\lambda. Comparing the distance spectral radius of two graphs reduces to comparing their Ψ\Psi-functions. The following theorem can be viewed as a key innovation in this paper to solve Conjecture 1.1.

Theorem 2.5.

Let G1,G2G_{1},G_{2} be two graphs satisfying the hypotheses of Lemma 2.3, with corresponding Ψ\Psi-functions Ψ1,Ψ2\Psi_{1},\Psi_{2}, respectively. If Ψ1​(λ)<Ψ2​(λ)\Psi_{1}(\lambda)<\Psi_{2}(\lambda) for every λ>2\lambda>2, then ρ⁡(G1)<ρ⁡(G2)\rho(G_{1})<\rho(G_{2}). More generally, if the strict inequality holds merely at λ=ρ⁡(G2)+1\lambda=\rho(G_{2})+1, then ρ⁡(G1)<ρ⁡(G2)\rho(G_{1})<\rho(G_{2}).

Proof.

Setting λi:=ρ⁡(Gi)+1\lambda_{i}:=\rho(G_{i})+1, we have Ψi​(λi)=1\Psi_{i}(\lambda_{i})=1. The assumption implies

Ψ1​(λ2)<Ψ2​(λ2)=1=Ψ1​(λ1).\Psi_{1}(\lambda_{2})<\Psi_{2}(\lambda_{2})=1=\Psi_{1}(\lambda_{1}).

Since Ψ1​(λ)\Psi_{1}(\lambda) is strictly decreasing by Lemma 2.3, we have λ2>λ1\lambda_{2}>\lambda_{1}, i.e., ρ⁡(G2)>ρ⁡(G1)\rho(G_{2})>\rho(G_{1}). ∎

Remark. By applying Theorem 2.5, we no longer compare the increment of the distance spectral radius via the entries of Perron eigenvector and the Rayleigh quotient of ρ⁡(G)\rho(G).

For every λ>2\lambda>2 and k⩾2k\geqslant 2, let θ>1\theta>1 be the root of θ+θ−1=λ\theta+\theta^{-1}=\lambda. Then

2.3 Balancing principles

We now derive two results: first, for a fixed total order and fixed number of parts, path lengths should be as balanced as possible (Lemma 2.8); second, enlarging the total order monotonically enlarges each part of the balanced partition (Lemma 2.9).

Lemma 2.8.

Let c⩾1c\geqslant 1 and N⩾2​cN\geqslant 2c be integers, and let k1,…,kc⩾2k_{1},\ldots,k_{c}\geqslant 2 be integers with ∑i=1cki=N\sum_{i=1}^{c}k_{i}=N. We denote (ki∗)i=1c(k_{i}^{\ast})_{i=1}^{c} the balanced partition of NN into cc parts, i.e., with q=⌊N/c⌋q=\lfloor N/c\rfloor and r=N−q​cr=N-qc, there are rr copies of q+1q+1 and c−rc-r copies of qq. Then for every λ>2\lambda>2,

∑i=1cΦPki​(λ)⩾∑i=1cΦPki∗​(λ),\sum_{i=1}^{c}\Phi_{P_{k_{i}}}(\lambda)\;\geqslant\;\sum_{i=1}^{c}\Phi_{P_{k_{i}^{\ast}}}(\lambda),

with equality if and only if (ki)i=1c(k_{i})_{i=1}^{c} is a permutation of (ki∗)i=1c(k_{i}^{\ast})_{i=1}^{c}.

Proof.

If (ki)i=1c(k_{i})_{i=1}^{c} is already a permutation of (ki∗)i=1c(k_{i}^{\ast})_{i=1}^{c}, then two sums are equal. Otherwise, there exist indices i≠i′i\neq i^{\prime} with ki⩾ki′+2k_{i}\geqslant k_{i^{\prime}}+2. We consider the operation: Replace (ki,ki′)(k_{i},k_{i^{\prime}}) by (ki−1,ki′+1)(k_{i}-1,k_{i^{\prime}}+1); the sum is changed only at these two indices, and the constraint kj⩾2k_{j}\geqslant 2 is preserved (since ki⩾ki′+2⩾4k_{i}\geqslant k_{i^{\prime}}+2\geqslant 4 gives ki−1⩾3k_{i}-1\geqslant 3 and ki′+1⩾3k_{i^{\prime}}+1\geqslant 3). Thus, the effect on these two indices is

(ΦPki−1​(λ)+ΦPki′+1​(λ))−(ΦPki​(λ)+ΦPki′​(λ))=Δ​Φki′−Δ​Φki−1,\left(\Phi_{P_{k_{i}-1}}(\lambda)+\Phi_{P_{k_{i^{\prime}}+1}}(\lambda)\right)-\left(\Phi_{P_{k_{i}}}(\lambda)+\Phi_{P_{k_{i^{\prime}}}}(\lambda)\right)=\Delta\Phi_{k_{i^{\prime}}}-\Delta\Phi_{k_{i}-1},

where Δ​Φk\Delta\Phi_{k} is defined as in (14). Since ki−1⩾ki′+1>ki′⩾2k_{i}-1\geqslant k_{i^{\prime}}+1>k_{i^{\prime}}\geqslant 2, and by Theorem 2.7 (ii), we know that Δ​Φk\Delta\Phi_{k} is strictly increasing in kk, we have Δ​Φki−1>Δ​Φki′\Delta\Phi_{k_{i}-1}>\Delta\Phi_{k_{i^{\prime}}}. So we get

ΦPki−1​(λ)+ΦPki′+1​(λ)<ΦPki​(λ)+ΦPki′​(λ).\Phi_{P_{k_{i}-1}}(\lambda)+\Phi_{P_{k_{i^{\prime}}+1}}(\lambda)\,<\,\Phi_{P_{k_{i}}}(\lambda)+\Phi_{P_{k_{i^{\prime}}}}(\lambda).

We conclude that the operation strictly decreases the sum ∑i=1cΦPki​(λ)\sum_{i=1}^{c}\Phi_{P_{k_{i}}}(\lambda).

Using the above operation repeatedly, we can turn any partition (ki)i=1c(k_{i})_{i=1}^{c} to a balanced partition. Indeed, we consider the quantity Q:=∑i=1cki2Q:=\sum_{i=1}^{c}k_{i}^{2}. Since ki⩾ki′+2k_{i}\geqslant k_{i^{\prime}}+2, we see that

Δ​Q=(ki−1)2+(ki′+1)2−ki2−ki′2=−2​(ki−ki′−1)⩽−2.\Delta Q=(k_{i}-1)^{2}+(k_{i^{\prime}}+1)^{2}-k_{i}^{2}-k_{i^{\prime}}^{2}=-2(k_{i}-k_{i^{\prime}}-1)\leqslant-2.

Thus, QQ strictly decreases under each step of the operation. Since Q⩾0Q\geqslant 0, the operation process thereby terminates at finitely many times. The terminal configuration admits no pair (ki,ki′)(k_{i},k_{i^{\prime}}) with ki⩾ki′+2k_{i}\geqslant k_{i^{\prime}}+2, i.e., it is a balanced partition of NN. Since each operation strictly decreased the sum, the starting value ∑i=1cΦPki​(λ)\sum_{i=1}^{c}\Phi_{P_{k_{i}}}(\lambda) strictly exceeds the final value ∑i=1cΦPki∗​(λ)\sum_{i=1}^{c}\Phi_{P_{k_{i}^{\ast}}}(\lambda). ∎

Lemma 2.9.

Let c⩾1c\geqslant 1 and N1<N2N_{1}<N_{2} be integers with N1⩾2​cN_{1}\geqslant 2c. Write (kj(i))j=1c(k_{j}^{(i)})_{j=1}^{c} for the balanced partition of NiN_{i} into cc parts, sorted in non-decreasing order. Then for every j∈{1,…,c}j\in\{1,\ldots,c\},

kj(1)⩽kj(2).k_{j}^{(1)}\;\leqslant\;k_{j}^{(2)}.
Proof.

We denote Ni=qi​c+riN_{i}=q_{i}c+r_{i} with 0⩽ri<c0\leqslant r_{i}<c. The sorted balanced partition of NiN_{i} is

(kj(i))j=1c=(qi,…,qi,qi+1,…,qi+1),(k_{j}^{(i)})_{j=1}^{c}=(q_{i},\ldots,q_{i},\,q_{i}+1,\ldots,q_{i}+1),

where qiq_{i} appears c−ric-r_{i} times and qi+1q_{i}+1 appears rir_{i} times. Since N1<N2N_{1}<N_{2} and cc is fixed, we have q1⩽q2q_{1}\leqslant q_{2}. If q1<q2q_{1}<q_{2}, then every entry of (kj(1))(k_{j}^{(1)}) is at most q1+1⩽q2q_{1}+1\leqslant q_{2}. Moreover, every entry of (kj(2))(k_{j}^{(2)}) is at least q2q_{2}. Thus, we get kj(1)⩽q1+1⩽q2⩽kj(2)k_{j}^{(1)}\leqslant q_{1}+1\leqslant q_{2}\leqslant k_{j}^{(2)} for every jj.

If q1=q2=qq_{1}=q_{2}=q, then N1<N2N_{1}<N_{2} implies r1<r2r_{1}<r_{2}. In this case, N1N_{1} has the partition {q,…,q,q+1,…,q+1}\{q,\ldots,q,q+1,\ldots,q+1\}, where q+1q+1 appears r1r_{1} times, and N2N_{2} has the partition {q,…,q,q+1,…,q+1}\{q,\ldots,q,q+1,\ldots,q+1\}, where q+1q+1 appears r2r_{2} times. Since r1<r2r_{1}<r_{2}, we see that kj(1)⩽kj(2)k_{j}^{(1)}\leqslant k_{j}^{(2)} for all jj. ∎

2.4 Proof of Theorem 1.2

Our goal is to prove that the minimizer G≅Pn,s+1¯G\cong\overline{P_{n,s+1}}. By Theorem 2.1, we know that |V⁡(G)|=n|V(G)|=n, and each component of G¯\overline{G} is either a cycle or a non-trivial path, and there are exactly s+1s+1 components being paths. Then we denote

H0:=G¯=Cℓ1∪⋯∪Cℓt∪Pk1∪⋯∪Pks+1,H_{0}:=\overline{G}\;=\;C_{\ell_{1}}\cup\cdots\cup C_{\ell_{t}}\cup P_{k_{1}}\cup\cdots\cup P_{k_{s+1}},

where t⩾0t\geqslant 0, ℓi⩾3\ell_{i}\geqslant 3, kj⩾2k_{j}\geqslant 2 satisfying Nc:=∑i=1tℓiN_{c}:=\sum_{i=1}^{t}\ell_{i} and Np=∑j=1s+1kj=n−NcN_{p}=\sum_{j=1}^{s+1}k_{j}=n-N_{c}.

Applying Lemmas 2.3 and 2.6 to GG and to Pn,s+1¯\overline{P_{n,s+1}}, we obtain

ΨG​(λ)=Ncλ−2+∑j=1s+1ΦPkj​(λ),ΨPn,s+1¯​(λ)=∑j=1s+1ΦPkj∗​(λ),\Psi_{G}(\lambda)=\frac{N_{c}}{\lambda-2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s+1}\Phi_{P_{k_{j}}}(\lambda),\qquad\Psi_{\overline{P_{n,s+1}}}(\lambda)=\sum_{j=1}^{s+1}\Phi_{P_{k_{j}^{*}}}(\lambda), (15)

where (kj∗)j=1s+1(k_{j}^{*})_{j=1}^{s+1} is the balanced partition of nn into s+1s+1 parts.

Claim 2.1.

Path lengths in H0H_{0} must be the balanced partition of NpN_{p}.

Proof of Claim.

Suppose for the contradiction that (kj)j=1s+1(k_{j})_{j=1}^{s+1} is not a permutation of the balanced partition (kj∗)j=1s+1(k_{j}^{\ast})_{j=1}^{s+1}. Now, we construct a graph G′G^{\prime} with G′¯:=Cℓ1∪⋯∪Cℓt∪Pk1∗∪⋯∪Pks+1∗\overline{G^{\prime}}:=C_{\ell_{1}}\cup\cdots\cup C_{\ell_{t}}\cup P_{k_{1}^{\ast}}\cup\cdots\cup P_{k_{s+1}^{\ast}}. Clearly, we have G′∈𝒢⁡(m)G^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}(m). For every λ>2\lambda>2, we get

ΨG′​(λ)−ΨG​(λ)=∑j=1s+1ΦPkj∗​(λ)−∑j=1s+1ΦPkj​(λ)<0,\Psi_{G^{\prime}}(\lambda)-\Psi_{G}(\lambda)=\sum_{j=1}^{s+1}\Phi_{P_{k_{j}^{\ast}}}(\lambda)-\sum_{j=1}^{s+1}\Phi_{P_{k_{j}}}(\lambda)<0,

where the last inequality holds by using Lemma 2.8. By the comparison principle in Theorem 2.5, we get ρ⁡(G′)<ρ⁡(G)\rho(G^{\prime})<\rho(G), which contradicts with the minimality of GG. Hence, we conclude that (kj)j=1s+1(k_{j})_{j=1}^{s+1} is a permutation of (kj∗)j=1s+1(k_{j}^{\ast})_{j=1}^{s+1}. In other words, we have |ki−kj|⩽1|k_{i}-k_{j}|\leqslant 1 for all i,ji,j. ∎

Claim 2.2.

We have t=0t=0.

Proof of Claim.

Suppose for the contradiction that t⩾1t\geqslant 1. Then Nc=∑iℓi⩾3​t⩾3N_{c}=\sum_{i}\ell_{i}\geqslant 3t\geqslant 3 and Np<nN_{p}<n. By Claim 2.1, we may assume that (kj)j=1s+1(k_{j})_{j=1}^{s+1} is the balanced partition of NpN_{p} sorted in non-decreasing order. Recall that (kj∗)j=1s+1(k_{j}^{*})_{j=1}^{s+1} is the sorted balanced partition of nn. Applying Lemma 2.9 to Np<nN_{p}<n, we see that for every jj,

mj:=kj∗−kj⩾ 0.m_{j}:=k_{j}^{*}-k_{j}\;\geqslant\;0.

Moreover, we have ∑j=1s+1mj=n−Np=Nc⩾3\sum_{j=1}^{s+1}m_{j}=n-N_{p}=N_{c}\geqslant 3, so at least one mj⩾1m_{j}\geqslant 1.

We now compare ΨG​(λ)\Psi_{G}(\lambda) and ΨPn,s+1¯​(λ)\Psi_{\overline{P_{n,s+1}}}(\lambda). Combining with (15), we get

ΨG​(λ)−ΨPn,s+1¯​(λ)=Ncλ−2−∑j=1s+1(ΦPkj∗​(λ)−ΦPkj​(λ)).\Psi_{G}(\lambda)-\Psi_{\overline{P_{n,s+1}}}(\lambda)=\frac{N_{c}}{\lambda-2}-\sum_{j=1}^{s+1}\bigl(\Phi_{P_{k_{j}^{*}}}(\lambda)-\Phi_{P_{k_{j}}}(\lambda)\bigr). (16)

By Theorem 2.7 (i), for every index jj, we have the following two cases:

  • •

    If mj=0m_{j}=0, then ΦPkj∗​(λ)−ΦPkj​(λ)=0=mjλ−2\Phi_{P_{k_{j}^{*}}}(\lambda)-\Phi_{P_{k_{j}}}(\lambda)=0=\tfrac{m_{j}}{\lambda-2}.

  • •

∑j=1s+1(ΦPkj∗​(λ)−ΦPkj​(λ))<∑j=1s+1mjλ−2=Ncλ−2.\sum_{j=1}^{s+1}\bigl(\Phi_{P_{k_{j}^{*}}}(\lambda)-\Phi_{P_{k_{j}}}(\lambda)\bigr)\;<\;\sum_{j=1}^{s+1}\frac{m_{j}}{\lambda-2}\;=\;\frac{N_{c}}{\lambda-2}.

By Claims 2.1 and 2.2, we have t=0t=0, and the path lengths in H0H_{0} form the balanced partition of nn, which yields H0≅Pn,s+1H_{0}\cong P_{n,s+1}, i.e. G≅Pn,s+1¯G\cong\overline{P_{n,s+1}}. This completes the proof of Theorem 1.2.

3 A new proof for the range s⩾12​(n−2)s\geqslant\frac{1}{2}(n-2)

In previous section, we determined the spectral extremal graph in the difficult case for the range 1⩽s<n−221\leqslant s<\frac{n-2}{2}, and thereby solved Lin–Zhou’s problem in Conjecture 1.1. The range s⩾max⁡{n−62,1}s\geqslant\max\{\frac{n-6}{2},1\} was already confirmed by Lin and Zhou [17] by using the Rayleigh quotient technique. In this range, we cannot apply the structural result stated in Theorem 2.1, so that we cannot use the previous lemmas for the increment analysis of Φ\Phi-functions on paths and cycles.

In this section, we provide another application of our approach developed in this paper. Applying the comparison principle in Theorem 2.5, we give a new proof of Lin–Zhou’s result for the range s⩾n−22s\geqslant\frac{n-2}{2} by combining Ψ\Psi-functions with walk enumeration. Counting the number of walks in a graph turns out to be powerful in studying spectral extremal problems; see, e.g., [18, 14, 6].

Before comparing the Ψ\Psi-functions, we need to bound the diameter of GG.

Lemma 3.1.

If GG is a graph on nn vertices with m>(n−12)m>\binom{n-1}{2} edges, then diam⁡(G)⩽2\mathrm{diam}(G)\leqslant 2.

Proof.

Suppose for contradiction that diam⁡(G)⩾3\mathrm{diam}(G)\geqslant 3. There exist u,v∈V⁡(G)u,v\in V(G) such that distance dG​(u,v)⩾3d_{G}(u,v)\geqslant 3. Thus uu and vv are non-adjacent, and N⁡(u)∩N⁡(v)=∅N(u)\cap N(v)=\emptyset. We now count the missing edges (non-edges) in GG. Observe that uu is non-adjacent to n−1−d⁡(u)n-1-d(u) vertices. In addition, vv is non-adjacent to d⁡(u)d(u) vertices of N⁡(u)N(u). So the total number of non-edges of u,vu,v is at least (n−1−d⁡(u))+d⁡(u)=n−1(n-1-d(u))+d(u)=n-1. Then we have e⁡(G)⩽(n2)−(n−1)=(n−12)e(G)\leqslant\binom{n}{2}-(n-1)=\binom{n-1}{2}, contradicting with the assumption m>(n−12)m>\binom{n-1}{2}. Thus, the diameter of GG is at most 22. ∎

Recall that e⁡(G)=m=(n−12)+se(G)=m={n-1\choose 2}+s. Since s⩾1s\geqslant 1, we have m>(n−12)m>\binom{n-1}{2}. Lemma 3.1 guarantees diam⁡(G)⩽2\mathrm{diam}(G)\leqslant 2, which implies for any two distinct u,v∈V⁡(G)u,v\in V(G), dG​(u,v)=1d_{G}(u,v)=1 if and only if u​v∈E⁡(G)uv\in E(G); and dG​(u,v)=2d_{G}(u,v)=2 if and only if u​v∉E⁡(G)uv\notin E(G). Let H0=G¯H_{0}=\overline{G} denote the complement of GG. We conclude that D⁡(G)=J−I+A⁡(H0)D(G)=J-I+A(H_{0}). Thus, the conclusions of Lemma 2.3 remain valid. Consequently, the Ψ\Psi-function of GG in Definition 2.4 is well-defined, and Theorem 2.5 is still applicable.

Note that e:=e⁡(H0)=(n2)−m=n−1−se:=e(H_{0})=\binom{n}{2}-m=n-1-s. For the range s⩾n−22s\geqslant\frac{n-2}{2}, we have e⩽n2e\leqslant\frac{n}{2} and

Pn,s+1≅e​P2∪(n−2​e)​K1.P_{n,s+1}\cong eP_{2}\cup(n-2e)K_{1}.

Using the Neumann series in Lemma 2.2, we expand the Ψ\Psi-function as

ΨG​(λ)=𝟏𝖳​(λ​I−A⁡(H0))−1​𝟏=∑k=0∞𝟏𝖳​A​(H0)k​𝟏λk+1.\Psi_{G}(\lambda)=\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}\bigl(\lambda I-A(H_{0})\bigr)^{-1}\mathbf{1}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}A(H_{0})^{k}\mathbf{1}}{\lambda^{k+1}}. (17)

Let wk​(H0):=𝟏𝖳​A​(H0)k​𝟏w_{k}(H_{0}):=\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}A(H_{0})^{k}\mathbf{1} denote the total number of walks of length kk in H0H_{0}.

Lemma 3.2.

Let H0H_{0} be a graph on nn vertices with n−s−1n-s-1 edges, where s⩾n−22s\geqslant\frac{n-2}{2}. Then wk​(H0)⩾wk​(Pn,s+1)w_{k}(H_{0})\geqslant w_{k}(P_{n,s+1}) for every k⩾1k\geqslant 1. If H0≇Pn,s+1H_{0}\not\cong P_{n,s+1}, then wk​(H0)>wk​(Pn,s+1)w_{k}(H_{0})>w_{k}(P_{n,s+1}) for all k⩾2k\geqslant 2.

Proof.

Note that s⩾n−22s\geqslant\frac{n-2}{2} and Pn,s+1P_{n,s+1} consists of some disjoint edges and isolated vertices. The isolated vertices contribute no walks, and each edge contributes exactly two walks of length kk. So wk​(Pn,s+1)=2​ew_{k}(P_{n,s+1})=2e for all k⩾1k\geqslant 1. In graph H0H_{0}, every edge admits at least two trivial walks of length kk that use only the two endpoints. Thus, we get wk​(H0)⩾2​e=wk​(Pn,s+1)w_{k}(H_{0})\geqslant 2e=w_{k}(P_{n,s+1}). If H0≇Pn,s+1H_{0}\not\cong P_{n,s+1}, then there exist three vertices such that x∼y∼zx\sim y\sim z, which yields many walk of length kk starting from xx (or yy or zz) and alternating between yy and zz. So wk​(H0)⩾2​e+1>wk​(Pn,s+1)w_{k}(H_{0})\geqslant 2e+1>w_{k}(P_{n,s+1}) for all k⩾2k\geqslant 2. ∎

Applying Lemma 3.2, if H0≇Pn,s+1H_{0}\not\cong P_{n,s+1}, then using the identity (17) gives

ΨG​(λ)−ΨPn,s+1¯​(λ)=∑k=0∞wk​(H0)−wk​(Pn,s+1)λk+1.\Psi_{G}(\lambda)-\Psi_{\overline{P_{n,s+1}}}(\lambda)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{w_{k}(H_{0})-w_{k}(P_{n,s+1})}{\lambda^{k+1}}.

Since w0​(H0)=w0​(Pn,s+1)=nw_{0}(H_{0})=w_{0}(P_{n,s+1})=n, w1​(H0)=w1​(Pn,s+1)=2​ew_{1}(H_{0})=w_{1}(P_{n,s+1})=2e and wk​(H0)−wk​(Pn,s+1)>0w_{k}(H_{0})-w_{k}(P_{n,s+1})>0 for all k⩾2k\geqslant 2, we get ΨG​(λ)>ΨPn,s+1¯​(λ)\Psi_{G}(\lambda)>\Psi_{\overline{P_{n,s+1}}}(\lambda). By Theorem 2.5, we obtain ρ⁡(G)>ρ⁡(Pn,s+1¯)\rho(G)>\rho(\overline{P_{n,s+1}}), as desired.
